children: Emma Tucker
1. FROM MY DESK

For roughly five hours during Xi Jinping's summit with President Trump last week, there was nothing on the agenda. The unusually long break was by design. Chinese officials had asked the U.S. to build more downtime into Xi's visit, including a private room inside the West Wing where the 73-year-old leader could rest with only his wife. His team also turned down a working lunch with Trump and left his arrival evening free.

The accommodations quietly shaped a visit that lasted barely two days. Behind the pageantry, Xi's team built his schedule around how long he could stand, how far he could walk and when he would need to stop, according to people familiar with the planning. The details around his physical condition are particularly consequential because Xi has concentrated extraordinary power in his hands while designating no successor.
Lingling Wei takes us behind the scenes of Xi's Washington visit and examines what the arrangements could mean for China's leadership.

In a new development in the FlyDubai attack, the United Arab Emirates said the co-pilot assaulted the captain with a crash ax-required to be stored on commercial flights-in an attempt to take control of the plane. The Emirati attorney general's statement signaled that the attacker likely didn't need to smuggle a weapon on board.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you're not subscribed, sign up here. If you're reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.
2. TODAY'S HEADLINES
The FlyDubai co-pilot had been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he held radical ideological views.
Fraternity membership has surged following years of campus backlash and administrative crackdowns, as recent scandals at schools nationwide are bringing renewed scrutiny to Greek life.
The Cornell rape allegations have cast an intense spotlight on Title IX processes.
Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson's progressive agenda has been hobbled by a string of violence, a budget deficit and turmoil inside City Hall.
In France, nationwide student protests demanding better school conditions have sparked clashes with riot police, with thousands arrested in recent days.
3. FROM THE MARKETS
AI is sucking in capital and squeezing the rest of the market, where stocks face higher interest rates and oil prices without a sexy technology story to sell, writes columnist James Mackintosh.
Paramount is poised to take control of Warner Bros. Discovery next week, leaving CEO David Ellison to integrate the media giants, cut billions in costs and manage nearly $80 billion in debt.
4. READ IT HERE FIRST
Prediction markets have a new class of high rollers.

Twenty-something traders with math and quant backgrounds are building firms that wager millions of dollars a week on platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket, often using AI tools and teams of bots to hunt for an edge. Among them are two former Jane Street interns whose little-known firm, Alcedine Technologies, has already become a top-10 trader across U.S. regulated exchanges and is now breaking into trades for hedge funds and other institutions. Gunjan Banerji and Katherine Long take us inside the young trading shops cashing in on the prediction-market boom.
The sneaker brand On wants to be everywhere without becoming ordinary.

The Swiss company has exploded to more than $3.5 billion in annual sales, but its next phase of growth comes with a risk: becoming so ubiquitous that it loses the premium status that helped fuel its rise. On is limiting shipments to retailers to keep shoes from ending up on sale and plans to hold the line on prices that average $170. Its founders had that strategy in mind from the beginning: Their first mood board featured an iPhone, an Eames chair and a Dyson vacuum cleaner. Our columnist Ben Cohen sat down with co-founder Caspar Coppetti to find out how On plans to keep getting bigger without getting cheaper.

6. SEE THE STORY
How a Boeing 737 MAX survived a nosedive near the speed of sound.

A violent chain of events pushed the FlyDubai jet into a 39-degree plunge, plummeting 17,400 feet in just 92 seconds. The dive and recovery subjected the aircraft to extreme speed and gravitational forces that snapped off part of its tail rudder. We visually break down the flight data to show how the plane stayed otherwise intact as two pilots traveling in the cabin took control and landed safely.
7. HAPPENING THIS WEEKEND
Saturday: Major League Baseball's Division Series begins, with four playoff games scheduled. College football's weekend slate includes No. 5 Ohio State against No. 14 Iowa.

Sunday: Brazil holds the first round of its presidential election, with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva facing a tight race against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro. The NFL plays in London, with the Indianapolis Colts taking on the Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.
Today's paper
8. THE NUMBER
1 in 5

That's the share of registered voters who hold an unfavorable view of both major political parties, according to our recent survey. Driven by economic anxiety and deep dissatisfaction with Washington, this bloc of "double haters" has expanded significantly since the last midterms. With more than 40% of these voters currently undecided or uncommitted, winning over this skeptical group could decide which party controls Congress.
9. AND FINALLY...
Meta's AI boss rocks a mullet and Crocs.

Mark Zuckerberg handpicked 29-year-old billionaire Alexandr Wang to lead artificial intelligence efforts at (Meta). The young executive brings an unconventional style to the tech giant, turning up to its development conference in a thrift-store camouflage shirt. True to his provocative reputation, he recently trolled an OpenAI executive on social media after she accidentally plugged Meta's new app in a television appearance.
10. BEYOND THE NEWSROOM

Opinion: The Supreme Court kicks off a new term Monday with a case ostensibly about climate change but with much bigger stakes. The real issue in Suncor Energy v. Boulder County is whether states and localities can turn federalism on its head to dictate policy for the rest of the country.
